utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Today is Monday, the 21st of August, 2006. I would like to greet all those present in this courtroom. Good afternoon, Mr. Mundis. Good afternoon to all Defence counsel as well as the new counsel who has recently been appointed and who is with us today. I would like also to greet the accused whom we already saw on Thursday and who were waiting for the -- this hearing to resume today. There are a number of decisions we have to issue orally. First, a decision about the admissibility of evidence regarding to the witness who testified on Thursday, last Thursday. All the exhibits are admitted - Mr. Registrar, you would only need look up the references given in the transcript last week - except for two exhibits. One exhibit offered by the Prosecution, it was the document attesting to the death -- the death certificate of a victim. It was not legible so we are going to mark it for identification only, and we hope that the Prosecution will be able to produce a certificate that is more legible regarding the name of the victim. The second exhibit that is not going to be admitted is an exhibit produced by Ms. Alaburic. I think it's Exhibit 71. It's the transcript of an interview with the witness. The witness said that this was not conformed to what he had said during the interview, and furthermore, the document had not been signed by the witness. This is a document 4D 0071. This Exhibit will not be admitted. But as for the other exhibits, they are all admitted, and later on, Mr. Registrar, you will give us numbers for these exhibits. We are also going to issue a decision that I'm going to read very slowly for the interpreters to be able to translate what I'm saying. This is a decision regarding the comments made by Mr. Ibrisimovic on the 3rd of July, 2006. Before the recess, on the 3rd of July, Mr. Ibrisimovic said that he regretted the fact that the Prosecutor had submitted to him three days before the appearance of witness Josip Manolic, that he has given him 12 documents, one of these documents being more than 400 pages long, and he stated that these documents were not on the 65 ter list of exhibits. The Chamber took note of this difficulty encountered by the Defence and would like to issue a decision on principle with regard to this issue. According to the decision rendered orally on the 3rd of July, and on the written decision of the 13th of July regarding the admission of evidence, the Trial Chamber would first like to recall that the Prosecutor has to disclose to the Defence all documents he intends to offer during the hearing in one of the working languages of the Tribunal as well as in the language of the accused, and this has to be done at least two weeks before the witness comes to testify. In order to allow the Defence to prepare its cross-examination efficiently and for a good administration of justice, the Trial Chamber believes that the Prosecutor should, as a general rule, only submit to the Defence -- only disclose to the Defence those documents that are included in the 65 ter list. Any other document that the Prosecutor deems relevant and for the case, any other document should be offered if that document appears to be absolutely essential for the case. At the time when these documents are disclosed to the Defence, the documents that the Prosecutor intends to offer during the testimony of the witness, from now on the Prosecutor will have the obligation to state very precisely which of these documents did not appear on the 65 ter list. During the testimony of the witness during the hearing, and during the production of various documents submitted to the witness, the Prosecution will have to inform the Chamber of the documents that were not on the list, and the Prosecution will then have to justify this and to explain to the Chamber why these documents are essential for the case. The Prosecutor is also duty-bound to explain and to justify why these documents were submitted to the Defence with such delay and why these documents were not included on the 65 ter list. This is the decision rendered by the Chamber, and I would like to invite the Prosecution to read it very carefully again after the hearing, but to sum up, when a document that was not on the 65ter list is submitted to a witness, then it is up to the Prosecution to explain to us and to justify why this document only is admitted at this specific time, and then the Prosecutor will also have explain in what way this document is absolutely essential for the case. This is for this decision. And tomorrow we'll issue or we'll deliver two rulings about documents related to Witness Manolic, and the second decision we'll deliver has to do with Witness Hujdur. We'll deliver these decisions tomorrow. Last week, at the end of the hearing, Mr. Praljak stated that he wished to take the floor and to deal with a logistical matter. I'd like to give the floor to Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I could speak at length about justice and fairness, but I will be brief. For a long time and very persistently documents have been gathered in order to attempt to challenge the indictment. A team consisting of many people has been working for me, facing numerous difficulties, as Your Honours have heard. It was very difficult to obtain these documents. My team has collected over 50.000 documents in a desire to arrive at the truth about the war. Not all of these documents can be used here because there are too many of them, but it was said that we do have the right to have computers which will make it possible for us to inspect those documents. All these lawyers with their brilliant legal minds are not fully familiar with all these events and their mutual interrelationships. They are not as familiar with these events as we are. This is a court of justice, and it is for the court to decide whether my rights can be exercised or not. The OTP, with Madam Carla Del Ponte, cannot do that, nor can the Detention Unit. So I ask Your Honours that such a simple, banal problem as the problem of a computer, which can be checked in a matter of ten minutes, should be resolved, that it should be put at our disposal so that we can select the most important documents to enable Your Honours to reach a fair and just judgement. I hope that you will issue a judicial decision to make a computer available as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, to complete the information provided by my client, I wish to hand over copies of our correspondence with the Registry regarding the putting into use of these computers which are such that Mr. Praljak cannot use the database he needs to use in order to assist us. Perhaps if the usher could hand these copies to you so that you can see that we are continuously discussing with the Registry, and no solution has yet been reached although it has been promised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges will confer about this tomorrow morning. As far as I'm concerned personally, let me recall that this computer problem, I mentioned it during the pre-trial stage, I mentioned it during the Srebrenica case, the preparation of that case that started today, and at the time the Registry told me that computers will be provided to the accused with certain memory for these computers, and I thought that this was to happen in the next few days, but I now find that six weeks -- six months later Mr. Praljak is telling us that he still does not have access to a computer that would allow him to manage these 50.000 documents. We'll discuss the matter with the other Judges. I cannot take a decision of my own accord. We need to discuss it with the other Judges, and as soon as -- tomorrow we'll tell you what we want to do about this, maybe write a memo to the Registrar, or maybe issue a decision that will make it an obligation to the Registry to provide these computers. So we'll tell you all about it tomorrow, because the Judges meet on a daily basis, and we'll deal with that specific issue in our meeting tomorrow. We now have a witness who should be cross-examined. Today, let me remind you, before I give the floor to Mr. Murphy, that the witness was examined during 5 hours and 36 minutes as part of the examination-in-chief. The Trial Chamber believes that the Defence should have eight hours. That is to say we'll hear the witness today, tomorrow, and also on Wednesday, part of Wednesday, because we have another witness who should be heard on Wednesday. I don't know how the Defence is going to organise itself, what will be the order of cross-examination, who will speak first. Mr. Murphy, you wanted to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's about the cross-examination of Mr. Beese. We have, of course -- we are aware, of course, of who will begin, and I think the Defence has reached a certain amount of agreement as to the areas to be covered, but there is one practical difficulty. Your Honours will recall that on the 13th of July of this year you rendered a decision on the admission of evidence dealing with certain documents that had been produced to Mr. Beese, and that decision, Your Honour, records that about 34 documents were put to the witness and tendered in evidence when he gave evidence on the 15th of June. But there were also, of course, a large number of documents - in all some 384 - ECMM documents which the Prosecution indicated they would like to be admitted. Your Honour, the difficulty is this: We would ask the Trial Chamber to -- to rule on the question of the admissibility of these extra documents, because there is a practical difficulty in the cross-examination as to how the Defence deals with them. If -- if they had all been admitted, then of course the Defence would have the obligation to cross-examine in a great deal more detail about these documents. If it were limited to the original 34, then the cross-examination might take a different course. But without the Trial Chamber's ruling, we are not quite sure how to proceed, and we certainly want to avoid being in a position where we have to come back and ask the Trial Chamber for further time, which might involve Mr. Beese in being recalled yet again. The Trial Chamber's decision of the 13th of July directs the Prosecution to submit a written motion requesting the admission of the additional documents in accordance with the Court's guidelines, and the guideline - guideline 6 specifically - tells us that the Prosecution may, within eight days of the witness's appearance, file such a written motion in the case of documents which were not put before the witness in court. Mr. Mundis will correct me if I'm wrong, and I hope that I'm not; it's not my intention to mislead anyone: I don't believe that any such motion has yet been filed, and in those circumstances, Your Honour, I would now invite the Court to rule that these documents, the additional documents that were not shown to Mr. Beese, should not be admitted in evidence. If the Trial Chamber is not yet ready to make that ruling, then, Your Honour, we would ask the Trial Chamber to note that it may be necessary for us to -- to ask for additional time depending on which of those documents may be admitted at some future time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Murphy, I've listened very carefully to what you've said. You've recalled the essence of our decision of the 13th of July, 2006. It was a very clear decision. We admitted the 34 documents that had been put to the witness, to the witness Beese, and as for the 384 other documents, we stated that if the Prosecution wished later on, after the hearing of the witness, if the Prosecution wanted to tender these documents, it was to follow and comply with a number of conditions according to our guidelines. As for the cross-examination, you have had the opportunity to access these documents, because a number of months have elapsed between the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination that will be starting today. Therefore, when you ask your questions to the witness, you can refer to these unadmitted documents, and later on you will be able to challenge them according to our decision if you wish that these documents should not be admitted. That's the way we have to go about it, because this decision that was given, it was delivered in between the cross-examination and the examination-in-chief. Once the witness has testified, if the Prosecution wants to tender a number of these 384 documents, the Prosecution will have to file a motion in accordance with the criteria we have outlined. And if you want -- if you, the Defence -- to challenge these documents, you will be able to do so and to explain why you believe that these documents should not be admitted. The principle of a fair trial will already allow you to ask any question you deem fit during cross-examination, questions based on the documents you have and documents you've had the opportunity to inspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My fellow Judge has just made a comment to me, but I think it's better if he says it himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it would be much better if very quickly - maybe tonight - the Prosecution were in a position to file a motion in order to make its position known to the Trial Chamber for the Trial Chamber to be able to rule on the admissibility of these documents before the end of the cross-examination of the witness. And this will make it so that it will not be necessary to recall the witness because -- a possibility that was mentioned by Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I'm sure you have understood what has just been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. We are endeavouring to produce a chart pursuant to paragraph 6 of the guidelines that were attached to the decision of 13 July, 2006. I will be quite transparent with the Chamber that, given the fact that the trial team's resources are dedicated to finalising the overall chart that is due to be filed on the 4th of September with respect to linking all exhibits to the witnesses, but particularly with respect to paragraph 6(A)(iv) of the guidelines, I'm not confident that the Prosecution will be in a position to file any such motion concerning the witness Beese in light of paragraph 6 of the guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, what we're asking here regarding these 300 documents and a bit more is for you to tell us through a motion that you should file very quickly to tell us why these documents will not be submitted to another witness, why it's not possible, because you could imagine that with another ECMM witness you could produce these documents. And second criterion, very important criterion, you have to explain why these documents or some of these documents are absolutely essential for the case. That's it. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been made aware of the fact that we decided that the Prosecution would be granted eight days, eight days to submit its conclusions. It's paragraph 6 of these guidelines. So we could be a bit more flexible, a bit more generous, and consider that the -- we should not take the recess into account, but nonetheless, that leaves you a very short period of time to comply, and you might be in a position to file this motion more quickly, because the Defence will have eight days to respond, and by that time, of course, the cross-examination would be completed, but the Defence is not duty-bound to use up these eight days. Mr. Mundis, a practical solution that you could envisage without interfering in the way you go about presenting your case is that you probably have other witnesses from the ECMM, and you might choose to use some of these -- the other documents for these other witnesses, and you might like to only keep here in this motion the documents directly related to Mr. Beese, and this would enable the Defence to prepare itself more efficiently. What do you have to say about this? What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As a starting point, Your Honours, the Prosecution is interpreting paragraph 6, and perhaps we're mistaken, but our interpretation of the guidelines, and particularly paragraph 6 in the English language version, says: "The Prosecution may, after the testimony of a witness and within eight days of his/her appearance before the Chamber, request the Chamber ..." Our interpretation of that, Mr. President and Your Honours, is that the phrase "after the testimony of a witness" would certainly include the cross-examination, and therefore our understanding - and we may be entirely wrong - is that that eight days begins once the testimony of the witness is complete, and that's not the direct examination but that refers to the cross-examination. And again, if we're mistaken in that, we will do what we can to rectify the situation. But in all honesty, in all transparency, we were interpreting this as meaning within eight days of the completion of this or any other witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're not wrong. You're quite right. It's just that my colleague, taking into account, like all the other Judges, that we are in a case which is in between the examination-in-chief and cross-examination and that this decision was rendered in the middle, in the interim, that we must find the right kind of procedure which would not be rigid and restricted by this eight-day rule. So you're quite right in your thinking. It is after the cross-examination that you will have eight days. But my colleague has just suggested that in anticipating these eight days and in making -- you could make this motion after tomorrow if that is possible. If not, then you can do it eight days later. But you're not wrong. You've understood it very well and done the proper analysis of our ruling. It's just that my colleague the Judge wanted to try, in accordance with the other Judges, of course, to give you more flexibility and to allow the Defence to deal with the problem raised by Mr. Murphy and to try and find a solution that would be a suitable one. But if you can't, we quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If I may suggest perhaps a middle course that might answer Judge Trechsel's concern as well as Mr. Mundis's. I wonder whether it might be possible for the Prosecution at least to provide us with a list of the documents to which their proposed motion would relate. In other words, those documents that they actually wish the Court to admit through Mr. Beese, and then to supply the other details required by guideline 6(A) at later time. That would address our concerns on the Defence side, because we would know which documents we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Mundis, you've just heard what Mr. Murphy said. He's just made a proposal. I think that I can agree, and so do all my colleagues, and that is that you should quickly tell the Defence, by mail or in any other way, what exhibits you're going to send in a written motion about after this eight-day period so that they know what to expect. That wouldn't be impossible, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I'm not mistaken, at the conclusion of the direct examination we -- we formally asked and tendered all of these exhibits to be admitted. I understand that we need to comply with the guidelines, and particularly paragraph 6 of the guidelines, in producing a chart. What we are endeavouring to do is to produce such a chart while at the same time complying with the Trial Chamber's order to produce the massive overall chart on the 4th of September. Whether we are able to do that in a short period of time, or even within eight days of the conclusion of this witness's testimony, I'm not standing here right now in a position to acknowledge. I will say that it's our position, the Prosecution's position, remains as we indicated on our filing of the 15th of June, and that is that the jurisprudence of the Tribunal supports our position, we submit, that it is permissible to admit all of these documents through the Witness Beese. We will produce the chart. We will endeavour to produce the chart within eight days of the testimony. If I can do that sooner, I assure you that we will do so, but we have formally -- to the best of my recollection, we have formally requested that all of the documents be admitted into evidence. My learned colleague is correct in that we anticipate additional ECMM witnesses coming to testify, and to a certain extent that may be part of the answer. Which documents would go with which subsequent ECMM witness is an entirely different matter and is partially what we're trying to accomplish pursuant to paragraph 6 of the guidelines. But I will stress again for the record that, as Your Honours are well aware, with this witness who is currently testifying, we spent, as Your Honour indicated, about five and a half hours and went through 34 documents with him. And we have an additional 384 documents to go, and at that rate it's going to require some 60 hours of direct examination to go through those documents at the same rate, on average. So we are endeavouring to do this, Your Honours. I give you my assurance that we will do so as quickly as we are able to do, but I can't, in all good faith, give you an assurance or a promise that it will be tomorrow or the day after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following on from Mr. Murphy's suggestion, we ask for all the documents, 384, so there's no reason to reduce their number. So the answer is -- that's the answer. We're now going to have the witness shown in without further ado, and we're going to discuss the problem. The Judges will discuss it. Ms. Alaburic, we've already lost half an hour, so perhaps we should let the witness come in, and I'm sure your questions are very important, but yes, you have the floor before the witness arrives.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's what I wanted to suggest, to use that time. If the -- since the Prosecution needed five hours to conduct the examination-in-chief on the basis of 34 documents, and according to what my learned colleague Mr. Mundis said, he would need 60 hours for the examination-in-chief on the basis of all the documents, pursuant to the ruling that the Defence has the same time, is accorded the same time as the Prosecution, and as we expect the cross-examination to be conducted on all the documents, we consider that the Court should make a ruling to accord more time to the Defence teams for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to discuss the matter tomorrow morning. We have taken note of what you've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to say good afternoon, to you, sir. We know each other. We saw each other during the examination-in-chief. Today we come to the cross-examination. The Defence counsels are going to ask you questions, so you will be testifying today, tomorrow, and part of Wednesday. There we have it. Now, who is going to start off? Ms. Alaburic, Counsel Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beese, good afternoon. My name is Vesna Alaburic, I'm Defence counsel from Zagreb, and I'm here as Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic. I'm going to ask you several questions grouped together, and I'm sure that your answers will help us throw more light and have a better understanding of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the first half of 1993 when you reported from that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, given that this was a particularly important convoy, this was an opportunity for the two sides party to this particular conflict to demonstrate their commitment to working together. I would have expected, sir, given the seriousness of the situation, to have seen more -- more significant government effort on the part of the HVO to see it through. I am aware that some military commanders attended the scene, but I believe there could have been more done politically and militarily to see it through to its conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in that context, in the context of the convoy of the 10th of June, I'd like to ask you whether General Petkovic, who was there and who did everything in his power to try to ensure the passage of the convoy, could have done anything more. So a concrete specific person in -- faced with that situation, could they have done more or not, or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe more could have been done, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in trying to explain the work of the European Monitoring Mission, you told us last time that in order to solve certain problems you contacted people whom you thought had the necessary power to solve those problems independently of the function and posts they held. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no. Can you direct me to a statement to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Last time you testified during the examination-in-chief when you explained who you contacted when you had a problem to solve, you said that you would contact people who had the power to do so regardless of whether they had that official position. Whether somebody was a minister or not a minister, that was immaterial, it wasn't important, but that you went to the man who you thought could solve the problem. But if you don't remember, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'll accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of the explanations you gave us as to who you contacted, and in view of what we've just said, would it be logical to conclude that you didn't contact General Petkovic in order to solve the many problems that arose principally because you considered that he didn't have the power to solve those problems? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically. We were directed to deal with the HVO Ministry of Defence and, in particular, Mr. Stojic and Mr. Bozic. So it would have been appropriate for us, under that arrangement, to see them first.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the registrar now show us document 4D 00100. Could that document be made available. It is an interview of my client, General Milivoj Petkovic, and it was published in the Zagreb newspaper called Vecernji List, a political daily, and it was published on the 16th of February, 1993. We don't have the document on our screens yet, but I hope we will do soon. We have translated the heading into English, and the last portion. My case manager Davor has been able to access the document. Well, not to waste time, perhaps it would be simplest, since I'm just going to focus on one particular passage that I consider to be relevant, for me to read it out. And I'd like to ask Madam Usher to place the English version, the English translation of that portion, on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As I said, it is an interview, the heading of which is "Guns belong to a smelting plant." And we're dealing with mid-February, 1993. That's the date. And General Petkovic, the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, says as follows, and I quote: "If we do not want the war to start again, for someone will always be discontented, and if all this military power is left on the territory of BH, it will be difficult to put it under control of any kind, and the war will always be top, actual. I think that the arms should be completely relocated from the whole territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or - and that is my proposal - to smelt all heavy arms in the Zenica steel plants. Consequently, the solution is in the complete demilitarisation of this state." Tell us, please, Mr. Beese, in view of your rich experiences in Bosnia-Herzegovina, would you consider this position to be the position of, as you said, a moderate officer who can contribute to peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must apologise. I don't think it's appropriate for me to comment on this. I can understand your position. I don't necessarily believe one can draw that conclusion from this alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Beese, I'd now like to ask you a few questions about your education and qualifications for performing the job of an ECMM

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you also told us that you left school when you were 18 and that you attended a military academy which lasted for 12 months and then attended a military training course for six months. And this was recorded on 3051, page 3051 of the transcript. Is that a correct interpretation of your education and training?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as far as your professional involvement is concerned, you've told us that you were in the army until 1978, that you worked for the Lloyd insurance company until 1982, and that up until 1988

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From that data, tell us, please, Mr. Beese, would it be well-founded to state that you have no knowledge of political sciences and sociology, social psychology, history, or any other science which would be important for analysing the political and general social relationships in a community?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's correct, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why you say it's not correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever I have worked, whether it has been in the Middle East or Africa or even in Europe, I've been required to understand the background to the issues that I was dealing with. In the Middle East I had responsibility for delineation or border, for relations between the two parties either side of the border. And in Africa I had to understand the economic background to the conflict I encountered in Mozambique as well as to understand the social issues of the time if I was to be successful. It is correct to say that at some stage I was responsible for a motor pool. That was only a small part of my role.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to what you wrote, in Mozambique you were engaged in the construction of railways, electrical power plants, and so on, and in this context you also dealt with economic issues. In Oman, you dealt with a motor pool, but there is nothing to indicate that you dealt with any kind of analysis or reporting. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you say which of the documents we discussed last time contains information showing that, before your arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you dealt with political analysis?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've been asked specifically that question. I can describe how I was required to analyse social, political, and economic issues in the Middle East and in Africa and how I was to report my findings to the chief of staffs of the military in Mozambique and Oman. That was part of my role.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, the documents that you created which we have seen as a rule do not contain information about your sources. So the credibility of those statements cannot be checked. When you put forward an evaluation, you do not say on which facts and sources your conclusions are based. Your reports are full of characterisations and alleged facts which cannot be checked because the source is not known. To the best of your knowledge, is this manner of compiling reports something that is in line with the proper and correct political analysis and reporting?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The account I submitted of my time in Bosnia is just that; it's an account. It doesn't set out to be proof of any particular position. I'm very happy to be questioned on anything I say. It is not indicative of the analysis I produce for my professional submissions. Those, such as those submitted to the ECMM, had supporting evidence provided by teams, by documents, by reports from third parties. They do not stand alone. They are supported by other people's submissions and views.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We will discuss your standpoints and analyses, but before that, if we could just clarify the following: What did you know about Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to your arrival there? When you explained how you were engaged, you did not say that you underwent any kind of training in the foreign office. May we conclude, then, that you were not given any training in the British Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was briefed only when I arrived in theatre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were informed of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina like the average citizen, from the media. Television and newspaper reports, but primarily television. Which television stations did you watch, and which reports were the source of your information about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The television stations were those broadcasting to Britain, that is the BBC and ITN, and the newspapers were those on sale in Britain, British newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you follow media from any other country?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were there different approaches toward the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the British media you watched, or were all the reports uniform?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports, as I continued to find during my time in Bosnia, were not always in accordance with the facts we observed in the field, and much of my responsibility in Bosnia was to report what I found, not what I read. It was important that I went in and had some information. There wasn't a great deal made available to me. The importance of my work was to find out exactly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. We're only trying to establish now what you knew about Bosnia and Herzegovina prior to your arrival there. Can you then tell us, at the time you arrived on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, what did you know about who the warring sides were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew who the warring parties were. I knew very little of the detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the aims of each of these warring parties?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you define for us now what these aims were? To put it simply, of the Croats, Serbs, and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe I can possibly give you an adequate reply in the context of the people in this room. The general understanding was a conflict to secure power.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, in answer to my clear question as to whether you knew what the aims of the warring parties were, you said that you believed you did. That's why I'm asking you to say very clearly what it was that you knew about the aims of the warring parties when you arrived on the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's very important to maintain a reasonably open view given that the media does not always have the answers. My account of my time, I hope, leads people through an experience perhaps to understand how I came to my conclusions. Those conclusions have not, to my knowledge, been published in a similar format elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I'm asking you about your view of the aims of each of the warring parties. My question is very simple. You can say you did not have a clear picture and we can move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but the answer is a complex one. It is much more complex in practice than asked. There was an attempt by a number of parties to secure their interest in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That as an aim is enough in itself. To understand the background to that and what particularly they wished in the future was much more complex. I'm afraid I can only give you an inadequate answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, your knowledge when you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina was based exclusively on media reports. These media reports presented in a very simple and simplified way the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The only logical conclusion is that your view of the situation could be reduced to some very simple standpoints.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered Yugoslavia generally with an open mind. I had an understanding of the degree of conflict. I was there to report on what I found, not necessarily to take a preconceived position. I didn't have a preconceived position when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I wasn't trying to say that. I just wanted to establish that at the time when you arrived on the territory of the former Yugoslavia you did not have a clear picture of the events and of the warring parties, but we'll move on. To the best of your knowledge, did the government of Great Britain have a clearly defined policy with respect to the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: UK government policy at the time was to support the international talks in Geneva with the aim of securing peace. There are other parts of the policy which are less clear and which I'm not qualified to speak on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What you just say, that you're not qualified to speak on these elements of UK policy, does this mean you're not qualified to reach conclusions about international political relations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My business is to report my observations and to reach certain conclusions and report them. It's not for me to interpret people's claims. You will see in my account that a number of claims made I found to be misleading, inappropriate. Therefore, accepting political comment on its own is not something I choose to do. I would rather understand the detail behind it before assessing whether or not I considered it to be appropriate or correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your briefing in Zagreb and Split in January, 1993, in view of the fact that the Monitoring Mission in May, 1992, left Bosnia-Herzegovina, what was the source of the information about events on the ground for the people who briefed you, if you know, as they were not there on the ground?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was very little detailed knowledge available. Most of it recounted actions that had occurred rather than the intentions of any one party.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please explain to me what a civil war is.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a legal definition of a civil war. The use of the phrase in my account gives the view that it is one people against the same people. There may be divisions within them for political, religious, or other reason, but it is essentially one people fighting themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. If I may ask for a position. What people do you have in mind? What people fighting what people? Within what people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, given -- given Bosnia-Herzegovina, the people of Herzegovina -- Bosnia-Herzegovina were fighting themselves. The people of Herzegovina fighting the people of Herzegovina. They came from perhaps fragmented communities within it, but they were from it. People fighting themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, as you were reporting about such sensitive matters and the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, I have to ask you whether you know that there were three nations living in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as members of other ethnic minorities who we will leave aside for the moment. Do you know that in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were three nations, and there still are three nations, not one?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a subject which I believe has been taken apart and put back together in so many ways. It was not entirely clear at the time outside Bosnia-Herzegovina what was happening. I don't believe there was sufficient government understanding from the nations who were involved, that is the Member States of the United Nations or the European Community. It was certainly not for me to interpret this kind of phraseology. My responsibility was to understand what was happening, why, and report it. That is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, are you trying to say that the Monitoring Mission of the European Community was not aware of the fact that there are three nations living in Bosnia-Herzegovina - Muslims, Serbs, and Croats - and that the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a conflict among those three nations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect, I think the question itself is a view.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the question is: Is there one nation or are there three nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina? And that's a matter of fact, not of opinion. If you can be assisted by the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which stated, and still does, that it's a state of three constituent nations; Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, as well as members of other national minorities. So it is an indisputable fact which has never anywhere been brought into question by anyone that Bosnia and Herzegovina is a state inhabited by three constituent nations. The fact that you do not know that there were and still are three nations living in Bosnia-Herzegovina throws a very interesting light on the entire Monitoring Mission and your reports. It seems quite incredible that you do not know who lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But as this is not a question, I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd quite like to answer that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I encountered a community in Bosnia-Herzegovina with an infrastructure to support it. Academically, one can argue at great length as to the number of nations that community comprised of, even as you could argue about the constituent parts of the European Community mission. We were one mission. We were monitoring one community. That community was fragmenting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What community were you monitoring?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Villages, towns, were part of a community. They contained elements of the three nations you mentioned, and others, but they were a community. They had lived hitherto in reasonable peace. The desire of the international community was, I believe, for them to continue to live in peace. I quite accept your point that there were evidently, as I discovered, three quite distinct nations, but the substance of that matter is not honestly of my concern except in terms of outcome, that is, how the three constituent parts later performed. But we were there to monitor a community.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I may conclude, then, that you were aware of the fact that there were and are three nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that these were Muslims, now called Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the tripartite talks in Geneva conducted under the auspices of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, at which the internal order of Bosnia-Herzegovina was discussed, were attended by representatives of the Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, and that is precisely the reason why they are called tripartite talks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we refer to them as talks, but I understand you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at who represented what nation at these tripartite talks. The Serbs, I assume you will agree, will represented by Radovan Karadzic. Are you familiar with the name of Radovan Karadzic as the leader of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Croats were represented by Mate Boban; is that correct? Can you tell us who represented the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, in your documents, in your reports, you vehemently opposed Alija Izetbegovic being treated as a representative of the Muslims and insisted that the Croats were wrong to treat Alija Izetbegovic as exclusively a Muslim representative rather than the representative of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have just told us that the Muslims were represented by Alija Izetbegovic at these talks, so it would be logical to conclude that Alija Izetbegovic could not have represented all three nations. Am I correct in concluding this?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand where you have found this in my statement. I have not formed an opinion or a conclusion on representation at that level.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You just told us here that the Muslims at the tripartite talks in Geneva were represented by Alija Izetbegovic. I only wish to stress your response and draw the logical conclusion that a person representing one of three warring nations cannot at the same time represent all three warring nations or the state in which those three warring nations live. This is a logical conclusion, whether you agree with it or not. So we can proceed to find out what these three warring nations living in Bosnia and Herzegovina were fighting about. Would you agree that the essence of the difference in the standpoints among the leaders of these three nations was the issue of the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or, rather, whether Bosnia-Herzegovina would be a unitary state, or whether it would be a loose confederation or a federation, or a state decentralised in some way? Would you agree with what I say?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That might be an academic view, but unfortunately, it's run straight through by the military operations on the ground. These were not consistent with that view. If the Serb party, for instance, had purely wished to organise itself in a particular way, it would not have secured territory in the way it did and forced refugees out from the area it considered to be its own.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I suggest that we test this by answering the following questions: What kind of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in your view, did the Muslims want?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect, this is not the substance of my reporting in Bosnia, nor my submission to the Court.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I were to conclude that the Muslims wanted an independent and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina which, as regards its internal organisation, would be organised as a unitary state according to the system of one man, one vote, and that this was the main political goal of the Muslims -- or, rather, of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is as I would have understood it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will take the break now. We will resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, we agreed what the object of the Muslims was. Now, briefly, I'd like to ask you -- and I'd like to ask you to be brief in your answers generally speaking. Let's look at the object of the Croats. Would you agree with me that it was their goal that Bosnia-Herzegovina should not remain in Yugoslavia but should be an independent and sovereign state and that it should be a composite social community in which each of the three nations on a given territory would be the majority nation so that the state should be a federation, confederation, an agglomeration of provinces or something along those lines? Would you agree with that assertion of mine?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, from the documents provided to us by the Prosecution and compiled by the European Monitors, we can conclude that the regional centre in Zenica sympathised or favourised the Muslim goals. Would you agree with that? Or, rather, that it favourised a unitary set-up for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regional centre in Zenica did not favour any one particular political position.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we show Prosecution Exhibit P 02051 to the witness now, please. And I'd like the witness, once the document has appeared on e-court, to take a look at it and to look at point 2, Mr. Beese, sentence number one. It says the declaration is worrying because it allows the confederation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and from that -- "The declaration is disturbing since it adopts HVO's wish for a confederate division of Bosnia-Herzegovina," which would lead us to conclude that you considered this to be worrying. So would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principal concern of the regional centre was that political dialogue should continue towards a conclusion, a satisfactory and peaceful conclusion. Its responsibility in the field was to report where that was going astray and where influences were being brought to bear that would wreck that process. So it is not for the regional centre to give a view on a political outcome except where a particular view and subsequent actions might destabilise the status quo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beese. My conclusions on the basis of your reports are different, but I think we'll clarify that. Now I'd like to ask you some questions about the Vance-Owen Plan. You wrote about the Vance-Owen Plan and spoke about it and so I assume that we'll agree very quickly on certain key elements in that plan. So listen to me carefully now, please, and let us establish certain standpoints with respect to the contents. The Vance-Owen Plan, from January, 1993, provided for a Bosnia-Herzegovina as a decentralised state; is that right? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on the Vance-Owen Plan in detail. It was what it was. In the end, it did not prove to be of great value.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Beese, do you know or do not know the contents of the Vance-Owen Plan? We're not going to comment on it. All I wish us to establish now is the contents. So are you aware and have knowledge of the contents of the Vance-Owen Plan as laid down in January, 1993? If not, say so and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with the practical aspects as they would be laid out in theatre rather than theory behind it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, for you to be familiar of the practical aspects of something, you have to know what that something is that leads to those consequences. So there's no problem if you tell us that you don't know what the contents of the Vance-Owen Plan is. Are you familiar with the contents of the Vance-Owen Plan? I ask you again not theory, just the contents of the plan.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us in principle what you know about the plan.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan was to offer the opportunity for a federal state - I think that's the right description of it - to be established whereby a number of provinces could be established with -- with lines agreed, frontiers agreed, if you want to use that word, between the three parties as a mechanism for the three parties to reach agreement on a political settlement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness document P 01043, Prosecution Exhibit. It is a document which is a map as part of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Mr. Beese, are you familiar with the fact that the blue areas on the map would be provinces 3 in the north, 8 and 10, that they were supposed to be provinces where the Croats would be in the majority, or to put it simpler, as Croatian provinces, designated as that, and that's why they were drawn into the map in blue?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen them with these colours on the map, and the establishment of provinces where one party had a majority did not or was not supposed to be the same as having ownership of them and powers that were absolute in them. You could call them, for convenience, Serb, Muslim, and Croat, to encourage parties to sign up, but that's not quite the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we're not talking about property rights. That's not what I wanted to suggest. We'll get to that later on. The provinces marked in white - 1, 5 and 9 - were designated in simple terms to be Muslim; is that right? Muslim provinces.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me when I say that the Muslims did not wish to implement the -- the Vance-Owen Plan? They didn't want to see it implemented, and that they considered it to be unfair?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some parties were much slower than others to come to agreement on it. Some never did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you be more precise, please? Which parties were much slower, and which never agreed to it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At different times different parties found that it suited their agenda. There were times when the military situation on the ground did not make it attractive to some parties. Therefore, at any one moment some might have cause to agree with it and some might not. It was a political solution that was attempted to be overlain over active conflict, so it didn't start off with a great deal of chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just one explanation. When you say "parties," I assume you mean the Croatian, Muslim, and Serb side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we show the witness Prosecution Exhibit now, please, 02168. The English version on page 7. For those following in Croatian, it is on page 4. This is what it says: "Quite obviously there are people not ready to accept the Vance-Owen Plan, especially among prominent military leaders who are conscious of the actual situation, the definite loss of Eastern Bosnia and the fact that the -- they will have to give over to the Croats large territories where the Muslims are the absolute majority, and there's no sense in that." That is a quotation from a report of yours to the ECMM, or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say mine. I can't see who transmitted this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When I say "your" I never mean yours personally but the Monitoring Mission. Since you spoke to us about many documents of the ECMM Mission of which you're not the author. So when I say "you," I mean the observer mission. Mr. Beese, in your opinion, the last part of that sentence, does it represent a political assessment of the ECMM, that there's no sense to that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intention is to suggest what will work as opposed to what will not work. It doesn't necessarily carry a political opinion, although it might be understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now, would you agree with me that the Muslims never clearly -- or stated loud and clear their opposition to the proposed Vance-Owen Plan, as the Serbs did, for instance, the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims were at a military disadvantage. It might not have been their wish to sign anything like the proposals that were put on the table. There were times when they came closer to signing because the pressure eased, but they were not keen on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Mr. Beese, if I were to say that you personally were opposed to the plan?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position was solely whether or not a plan would actually work. The possibility of trying to implement a plan practically at a time of open conflict was of grave concern to me. It doesn't matter whether I think it is going to be a good plan or a bad plan. That is not my concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, from that statement of yours that you considered the plan was not a good one as long as the conflict continued, did you consider that the conflict should cease first for the sovereign nations to be able to decide their future? Is that what you meant? Was that your position?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To clarify, it is only possible to implement a plan acceptable to all parties given certain conditions in the field. The conditions were not there, and it was our understanding from the actions of some of the parties that although they had perhaps signed to it, they were not keen to implement it as signed. In other words, military activity in the field was at variance with the desire to sign this agreement in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, the regional centre in Zenica was also opposed to the Vance-Owen Plan, and this can be borne out by the following document, so I'd like that document to be shown the witness. It is P 02737. And in that document, in point 2, it says the following: "The Vance-Owen Plan could have been an acceptable transition, but no chance was given to the future of that country. The next step after recognition of autonomy would be independence after a referendum, and gradually there was ethnic cleansing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the end of the French translation. May I ask you, Ms. Alaburic, to slow down a bit because of the difficulties with the translation, and I would be very grateful to you. Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I apologise to the interpreters. It wasn't my intention to speed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what I've just said, anybody unbiased reading the

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Vance-Owen Plan was not acceptable to the ECMM because it did not ensure a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The writer of this report, in this case a professional diplomat, was giving his view that the plan as proposed was a halfway house to nowhere and that perhaps more ill could come of it than good. I think he was duty-bound to give his feelings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, from the ECMM documents, it would emerge that it was considered a much more acceptable solution to assist the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which as you consider was the sole force fighting for a uniform state, and that it should be helped by lifting the embargo, because that would enable it to fight for the interests of the Muslim people and win them. Would you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Comment on the lifting of embargo would have been made as a suggestion towards stabilising the region. There were opposing views about the rearmament of the central government. Some felt it would destabilise, some felt it would stabilise, but it certainly was another possibility to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beese. Now, during the examination-in-chief with respect to the alleged numerous ultimatums that the HVO made on the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you said that you remember two of those ultimatums, and you mention the dates. The 16th of January was one, and the 14th of March was the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the alleged January, 1993, ultimatum, you told us during the examination-in-chief that the commander of the brigade of the BH army in Mostar - and you didn't remember what his name was - informed you on the 15th of January about an ultimatum by the HVO demanding that the units of the BH army in the Croatian provinces according to the Vance-Owen Plan should be placed under the control of the HVO up until the 20th of January, 1993. Now, in respect of that statement of yours, I would like to ask you to explain to us, what were the consequences of the BH army not complying with that condition stipulated? What would have happened?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was, to my understanding, no official word on what would have happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us this: The commander of the BH army brigade, was he the sole source of your knowledge about that alleged ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you ever later on see any decision which would have the force of an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can I ask you to ask that one again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that this oral information given you by this officer of the BH army, that that was the sole source of your information at the time. Now, I'm asking you whether ever at a later date you saw any decision whatsoever in which that ultimatum was made to the BH army. Any document about an ultimatum, the alleged ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of January, 1993, on that date, did anything vital happen in relations between the HVO and the BH army, or did those relations continue as they had been up until that date?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relations continued to be strained.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Without any revolutionary changes in those tensions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as regards the second alleged ultimatum, on page 93 -- or, rather, in 1993, in paragraph 310 you wrote the following: You said that that new ultimatum that was mentioned by Mr. Arif Pasalic on the 14th of April, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what demands were made of the BH army on the basis of this new ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The demands as I understood them were for the BiH forces in the Dreznica valley to lay down their arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So in one area, in one locality. Thank you. Tell me, please, from your later knowledge about the events in April, 1993, would you agree with my following assertion, that the rumours going around by members of the BH army about an ultimatum in April, 1993, were in fact an alibi for military action which the Muslims were then able to portray as a counter-offensive?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I could have made that connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could the witness be shown Prosecution document P 09494, which is a communique dated the 1st of May, 1993. The witness said something about this document. It's on transcript page 3149. Mr. Beese, with respect to point 3 of that public statement, it says: "The utmost concern was expressed with respect to the continued aggression by Muslim units against the Croatian civilian population, and this is based on information from Konjic, Jablanica, Zenica, Travnik, Busovaca and Vitez." Mr. Beese, according to what you knew then, or what you learned later, is this part of the statement true or not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not consistent with my understanding of what was happening in theatre at the time. There were events, relatively confined minor events that could have been seen to be Muslim aggression, but they should be seen in the context of HVO military advances and attacks. To describe Muslim aggression when they were but pin-pricks against the background of open hostility is not valuable.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, if I understand you correctly, you think that these military activities by Muslim units were a counter-offensive or, rather, a response to HVO activities?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were, I understand, response.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown document 4D 00081. I apologise to the witness, but we have not yet received translations of the BH army documents we have, so we will have to use the version in B/C/S. I will try to read to you what I feel is relevant here. The document we have on the screen is an order issued by Mr. Arif Pasalic on the 7th of April, 1993, and in point 1 of the order it says: "Take all necessary measures and actions in the spirit of our earlier order about putting units into full combat readiness as ordered." I will leave out the remaining points, and I will draw attention to the last sentence in capital letters: "For a free Bosnia-Herzegovina - until final victory!" I will put my question after we have seen the whole set of documents. The next document, 4D 0083. 4D 00083. We have the B/C/S version because the translation was not ready. This is a combat report issued by the command of the Lisanj Battalion. It is signed by Esad Ramic, and it refers to Konjic and Jablanica. I wish to draw attention to a sentence contained in lines five and six from the bottom. I quote: "This time there is no stopping. We will press on until the final victory, because we are now convinced that the HVO is an enemy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." The greeting at the end is again: "Until the final victory!!!" with three exclamation marks. Could the witness also be shown document 4D 00084.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges take note of the fact that the witness is not in a position to identify these documents. He doesn't know these documents. So you probably have a question to put to him because there is probably a point to all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain. I do not wish to tender these documents into evidence at this point precisely because the witness is unable to identify the documents or the authors. However, these are documents issued by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they can be very valuable to clarify the events that took place in April, 1993, and especially the ECMM reports on these events in April, 1993. I feel that the responses to the events described in BH army documents can be very important in assessing the credibility both of this witness and of the ECMM documents. That's why I feel it's much better to show the documents of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina than to put questions in the abstract. I believe that after showing these documents the witness may get a different picture of events in Bosnia and Herzegovina in April, 1993. That's why I ask that I be given leave to show these documents to the witness. I will go through them very quickly and not spend a lot of time on them. Thank you. Document 4D 00084 is also an order issued by Mr. Arif Pasalic, dated the 16th of April, 1993. And in item 1 it says: "Continue combat activities in your zones." Could we also show the witness 4D 00086. 4D 00086. This is again an order issued by commander Arif Pasalic, dated the 17th of April, 1993, in which he orders a continuation of offensive combat activities, and this has been altered by hand into "defensive." He says that initial successes must be exploited to the maximum. In order to save time, I will skip over several BH army documents, and I will ask that the witness be shown 4D 00094 as the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a question with regard to this document. What is your position as to this handmade change? Is it a change that was made by General Pasalic or by someone else later on? And either way, what reasons do you have to uphold this?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to the alterations because they are evident to the naked eye, and anyone holding this order in their hand will certainly notice this alteration. As you do not have a translation and can read neither the word underneath nor the word on top, I thought it was correct to say that the word "offensive" was typed and that it was corrected in hand -- by hand into "defensive." That's the only reason I mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. Actually, this has not escaped me. By hand, yes. The question is, which you have not answered, whose hand? General Pasalic's hand, or someone else's hand? This cannot be seen by naked eye.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot know who altered this word by hand. This document comes from the archives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can only draw the following logical conclusion: A document referring to a continuation of offensive combat activities would be in favour of members of the HVO and people involved in any way in the activities of the HVO, and perhaps also the accused. So to make this alteration would certainly not be in my interest or the interest of the accused here. It seems quite hard to believe that anyone from the Croatian side would make this alteration. If one tries to conclude logically in whose favour this alteration could be made, it can only be made in favour of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, to put things very simply, the Muslims, because it was their usual tactics to describe even offensive combat activities as defensive. Ten or 15 years later, when Your Honours or somebody else sees a certain document, not knowing what lay behind it, you might really believe that these were defensive and not offensive actions. I know my answer cannot satisfy Your Honour's question, but I really do not know who made the alteration. In any case, I feel it's indicative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The question, of course, remains open whether it was General Pasalic himself who made the alteration, or whether it was someone else who, as it were, forged the document, falsified it later on. This we just must leave open, and this is the value we attach to this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown this document, which is information issued by the commander of the 4th Corps on a meeting with the European Monitors, and it's a meeting which you yourself described during your examination-in-chief, and it took place on the 8th of May, 1993. I wish to draw your attention to the second paragraph of this information, which says, I quote: "The representatives of the European Community demanded that the European Community be allowed access to Konjic and Parsovici," and in brackets it says "the surrounding settlements." Mr. Beese, during your examination-in-chief you did not mention that you demanded in imperative terms entry to certain settlements in the Konjic area. Was this an accidental oversight or did you have some reason for not mentioning it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I be clear? We have a series of documents here which you're going to pose some questions to me. This question relates solely to this document? I'm sorry, I have seen four --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's just about this document and then I'll put another question concerning all the documents. Did you fail to mention the fact that you demanded entry to certain places in the Konjic area on purpose, or was it just an oversight?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not specifically have commented. Access to all areas was implicit in the agreements between the parties, and access was not given by some of the parties. I didn't have to say it on a particular day. It was implicit in the business of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether before this members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina denied you access to certain places in the Konjic area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had had some difficulty in the Turija pocket south-east of Konjic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would now like to show another document. It's a Prosecution document, and then we'll round off the topic of April and Konjic. It's document 01911. It's an ECMM document about the current crisis in Jablanica. In point 5 it says that Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or, rather, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is trying to take strategic military positions in Zlatar to the east of Konjic, block the communication from Prozor to Jablanica, and expel all HVO units from Jablanica and Konjic. This is under 5, "Current situation," or "Present situation."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, what was the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, my question concerns all of these documents. After you have seen all these documents showing that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina planned offensive combat activities and that it did so as early as early April, 1993, and that in April, 1993, members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina really did take Konjic and numerous villages around Konjic, and everything you knew about the events in April, 1993, would you agree that this was a Muslim aggression on territories previously inhabited or controlled by Croats?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a yes or no. I am duty-bound, I think, to explain to the Court in this context what is meant, because the documents that you have produced here could be seen to be something other than what I suspect they are. Given that the HVO had advanced on Jablanica with the strongest possible forces from Prozor and from Doljani, given that the HVO was attempting to move from Prozor north-east towards Fojnica, and because that was difficult, also north through Kostajnica to Fojnica. These would be reasonable measures to take to protect the territory that was being moved against by the HVO. I can't accept that these in themselves amount to proof of offensive action. They would be the measures you would expect of an army that was under considerable pressure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
