utterances.text: Would I be right in concluding that all these activities of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in April, 1993, you feel are justified?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't used the word "justification," of course, very carefully. I see nothing from the documents you've shown me and kindly explained to me that give details about what aggression you expect to see from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is considerable mention of people needing to get their kit on and get ready for combat and to fulfil their instructions to any particular degree, but they don't suggest to me any particular plan. But I do understand, from what I could see and do know, that there would have had to have been a military response to HVO aggression across the front, and this would have been perfectly understandable and expected. That's not the same as accepted or justified.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: - I apologise if I'm wrong - but I have not found any critical remarks about the actions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or any criticism of their activities, unlike the sea of very cynical comments referring either to individual Croats, Croatian officials, the HVO, and I will be happy to be proved wrong. So can you show me whether in any document of which you are the author there is any critical comment about Alija Izetbegovic, Arif Pasalic, or any other officer of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or any Muslim politician.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will see, if you read the account from beginning to end, there is considerable comment on Muslim or armija or Bosnian activity which I find to be wrong, incorrect, unjustified. Considerable comment. You will also see through my account, which at the time it was written was not produced for this purpose, I stress the need for the monitors to remain neutral as best they can, unbiased in their dealings. If I have condemned in my writings, or it is interpreted that way, that I find one party's methods or actions to be reprehensible, then I have done so. The greater weight of evidence, I believe, condemns one party of greater aggression than the other. That is not what I heard from the party concerned, and I find that the use of these five or six documents put here go to support a position that the Muslims were aggressive. They do not do that to me at all. I do not take that to be the view, and I find this to be consistent with the propaganda that I experienced at the time in 1993 in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I'm not familiar with any statements of yours containing such critical comments on Muslim actions, could you please tell us what statements those are?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I comment on the activities of some irregular elements, particularly in the Klis region. I comment on the activities of unknown but certainly aligned to Muslim forces in Zenica on prisoner exchange. I give comments on the political personalities in Zenica with whom I can hardly have been said to agree on a number of occasions. I think you will find many examples of where I comment on their disorganisation, their inability to determine who truly represented them. You've mentioned Mr. Izetbegovic. Many laid claims to running the show. Few managed to deliver. They did not measure to the HVO in terms of organisation or equipment or planning, but certainly what I see here is a desperate response to wholesale aggression. Interestingly, the dates that you show some of these messages immediately follow the unprovoked shelling of Jablanica and the destruction of Ahmici. They can only be seen to me, without other evidence, to be a natural progression, something that I believe the HVO initiated rather than the other party. I'm sorry if you haven't drawn the same conclusions from my account.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I think your standpoint toward the warring parties is clear now from what you say and that your sympathies were with the Muslims. This is understandable in a way, but I think it's very important when a European monitor shows sympathies for one of the warring sides, this is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please, because I'm lost here. You're saying that sympathies lie with the Muslims whereas as part of his mission he was supposed to be neutral. Mr. Beese, the Defence counsel is saying that you were sympathetic to the Muslim side. What do you have to answer to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only report on what I experienced. I have no sympathy with one side or the other. I do have concerns for aggressors. I have some understanding with the victims of aggression. I do not have sympathies that are displayed professionally for one or the other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, what can -- what allows you to say that he had sympathy with one party? Because he's just said that he was neutral.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we put P 02620 to the witness. This is a report by the deputy of the head of the Monitoring Mission for political issues, Mr. Anderson, about the meeting with Ejup Ganic in Geneva. Ejup Ganic was the deputy of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. In this report, in point 7(A), it says, I quote: "The special observations of the ECM Mission were the following: The Muslims have to adhere to human rights, norms with respect to the Croatian and Serbian minorities in areas under Muslim control if they don't want to risk losing the understanding of the international community." Since one cannot lose something one does not have, it's logical to conclude that the Monitoring Mission is here declaring that the international community has understanding for and is supporting the Muslim side in the conflict. Also, from the documents we read today, when we compare the comments made about the wishes of the Croats to have a federal organisation and the wishes of the Muslims to have a unitary state, when one looks at Mr. Beese's comments, who never uses any negative adjectives when talking about the Muslims, whereas whenever he mentions the Croats he always as a rule includes negative comments, ranging from their shoes, vehicles, the way they speak, and many other elements important in communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: least not in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beese, what do you have to say to that, to those observations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If -- if I could, Your Honour, I'd like to see this point 7 on the screen. I'm too high on the document at the moment. Your Honour, I understood there was a question on point 7. I'm looking at point 6, which appears to be the last point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On e-court we don't seem to have point 7. Perhaps we can put it on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a document, to the best of my recollections, but I can check this out. It is a Croatian and English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think you are -- I think you are referring to a different document than the one that is on the screen. Perhaps if you would identify the document, not just by the number but by date and what else belongs to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I do that, may I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, what quotation are you interested in precisely, because I quoted several documents, and I don't know what you're referring to now specifically. Could you specify, please? 2620, the Ejup Ganic meeting in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I was at a loss to keep up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we place the Croatian version of this text on the ELMO, please. Then I'll be left without it, but it will enable us all to follow. I will mark in red the portion that is relevant. It is Prosecution document -- a Prosecution document, and the red portion is the portion I quoted from. Point 7. It says: "Especial comments of the ECMM included the following: "a. The Muslims have to adhere to international rules on human rights in view of the Serbian and Croatian minority in the areas under Muslim control if they do not wish to risk the loss of understanding and support from the international community." So the members of the ECMM, in talking to the vice-president, Alija Izetbegovic, clearly stated and expressed their understanding and support to one of the parties in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't make that connection. This would have been a normal comment that all parties need to respect human rights in their areas. I don't see the bias in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps -- perhaps one should also note that the text speaks of understanding, not of sympathy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel Alaburic. All the Judges are unanimous in noting that that sentence is -- or phrase is not -- does not relate to sympathy. It is just that the Muslims should respect minorities, whether they be Serbian or Croatian, in their -- in the area under their control. No sympathies in that article. I don't know how you understand the text, but that's how we understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not use the word "sympathies" in respect of this text, because the important words here are "understanding," and "support." Those two words. And in this sentence it says that the Muslims, if something were to happen, would forfeit the understanding and support of the international community, which means that at that point when that is being stated the Muslims do enjoy the understanding and support of the international community. Now, that statement by the ECMM to the vice-president --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can change the words and the text will apply to the Serbs or Croats, but you can draw your own conclusions and the Judges will take note of what has been said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Now, as far as the word

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: comparative analysis of how many Croatian bodies and officers or soldiers he mentioned compared to the Muslim ones and how he portrayed one and the other and what qualifications he used to describe one set and the other set, we don't have enough time to do that. But if we were to be able to do that and go into all the documents we could analyse that. But I've spent quite a lot of my time or, rather, my colleagues' time already, so I'll have to interrupt the cross-examination there. Mr. Beese, thank you for your answers and for your cooperation. And I also thank the Chamber for listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, Mr. Beese, you've heard what the Defence counsel said. He quoted a number of paragraphs from your writings. 23 -- paragraph 23 where you say that the Croats are arrogant, nationalist, and so on and so forth. And paragraph 594, Counsel Karnavas went on to list a number of points. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I report or the conclusions I reach are the product of what I observed. If officials in the HVO had pictures of Ante Pavlovic on their walls, who was known to be an extremist, if the rocks around Herzegovina have the U symbol of Ustasha on them, I'm bound to draw some conclusion. These are only some examples. I'm quite prepared to discuss many of these and how I reached the conclusions, but it doesn't mean to say I'm biased in my dealings, and I make great pains through the document to express how we needed to be to be credible. And those aren't because I wished to be seen to be something and be something else. That is the business. That is the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your answer is -- well, we see Mr. -- We've heard your answer but Mr. Praljak is on his feet. We won't enter into that discussion, we're going to lose a lot more time. You will have an opportunity to come back to that. But let's have the next Defence counsel. Who is it? Yes, please go ahead, madam. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to say at the outset that I will conduct the cross-examination, and perhaps after that Mr. Coric will use his own time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Beese. My name is Dijana Tomasegovic Tomic, I am a lawyer from Zagreb, Defence counsel for Mr. Valentin Coric in this case.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I have a series of questions to ask you too, but as we've just got into this whole discussion of bigotry and bias and prejudice, I would like to follow on from that and ask you to help me out here. As far as I understood my learned colleagues and Their Honours a moment ago, it was not your attitude about officers that was a case in point but your attitude towards the Croatian people. As far as I understood your answers to my learned colleague Ms. Alaburic, you said that you had a short briefing, and after that you took up your duties straight away. You came to Zagreb, and that's what you've said in the examination-in-chief. You went to Siroki Brijeg, and you arrived in Siroki Brijeg in January, did you not? The beginning of January. On the 8th of January, I believe.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you the following now: I'm sure you will remember an event that took place when you took up your duties in the first two or three days of your mission there when, in the Republic of Croatia, you attended a memorial meeting, a ceremony to -- about the death of the ECMM monitor. Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless I'm very much mistaken, one or two days after your arrival in the Republic of Croatia, and you were there for the first time in your life, you describe the people present in a church for a commemorative service, and as it was a Catholic church I assume most of them were Catholics, were Croats, so you described them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not clear quite what the issue is here or what the question is. Is it that I --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: What -- who does your description refer to, and is it obvious that it is a description of the people who were in the church when you were there? And they were the local population, and they were in the Catholic church where the commemorative service was being held, so I assume that they were Croats. Is that right? And my question is am I right in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I want to ask you in respect of that is this: As far as I was able to understand, this is an event that took place just a few days after your arrival in Siroki Brijeg and your first sojourn in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. Of course the writing of this was not --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I had a reasonable understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you have this reasonable understanding from? Did you look at statistical data, how many people worked in Germany, for example, or their origins? Did you know where their roots were? How many people did you talk to? Can you answer those questions or not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I had reasonable discussion with the people with whom we stayed, with interpreters, with officials.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Which officials, and how many inhabitants from Herzegovina work in Germany, for instance?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you figures, and the --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] With Your Honour's permission, then, I'd like to ask Mr. Beese whether in 1994 he had statistical and demographic data.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'd just like to ask you the following or, rather, to draw a comparison that I'd like you to clarify. As far as I understand it, Mr. Beese on several occasions told me today and my colleagues that he doesn't see where our line of questioning is leading. Am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see a tremendous amount of indignation from you, which I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, your interpretations and descriptions seem to be biased to me. As somebody who is a Croat and from those areas, I'm astounded with this type of position on the part of an ECMM. Now, I'd like to ask a hypothetical here. In your examination-in-chief you said that you were in the service of the Sultan of Oman, and that after that you were in Northern Ireland within the British army there to keep law and order. Now, my image of you -- if I were to give my image of you, description of you as you did of the Croats, that if I could say hypothetically that because you were in the service of the Sultan of Oman, for example, you were -- your sympathies lay with the Muslims because they paid your salary or, rather, that you have something against the Catholics because the Irish are Catholics and you were in the British army and established law and order in Northern Ireland. I don't think that would be in order. I don't think that would be proper, and I'm sure you'll agree with me that that kind of conclusion would be completely biased and partial about you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on to another topic. I think we've exhausted the previous one. And I'd like to go back to an event which you described in the examination-in-chief when asked by the Prosecutor. It is the event of the 5th of the -- of the 5th of February of 1993, when, according to your knowledge, in Ante Zvanic Street, from their flats in Mostar, 14 people were taken away towards the separation line or demarcation line in Stolac with the Serbs. You remember speaking about that? You know the event I mean?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, linked to that event you stated during your testimony that on the 6th of February you visited the flats and building or, rather, the building where those flats were located escorted by Mr. Ray Lane. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you also said something different with respect to that event. You said that Ray Lane and Paul Ronksley decided to go to Mostar to discuss the case with officials there while you and your colleagues went to Stolac to talk to eyewitnesses to the event. Do you remember having said that as well?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have to take a break. Maybe if you have a very short question, you can put it to the witness and then we'll have a break. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I need five minutes, if possible, and that would round off this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In that case, we'll take the break now, and we'll resume 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, before the break we were referring to an event of the 5th of February, 1993. We have discussed two quotations or, rather, two statements made by you during your direct examination, and also an ECMM report of the 19th [as interpreted] of February, 1993. I now wish to continue. I apologise. I believe in the transcript it says the 19th of February. This was in fact the 10th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I now wish to move on to my next question. In your statement, you also said that in connection to this event you also spoke to Mr. Valentin Coric. Can you tell us where and when you talked to him?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think my account will describe a meeting in March, I think March or April, when I asked Mr. Coric how the investigation was proceeding and whether there had been any outcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Coric then tell you who was in charge of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, though I would have understood that it would have been his responsibility as much as anyone else's to have investigated.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Talking of responsibility, please tell me, in your opinion if Mr. Coric had initiated an investigation and if persons subordinate to him had carried out an investigation, would you have thought that he had fulfilled his duty? You have a military background, so I wish to know if he had ordered an investigation to be carried out and if the investigation was indeed carried out, would you have felt that he as a commander had fulfilled his duty?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm missing something. I don't quite understand. I was given to understand that Mr. Prlic had given a commitment to open an investigation. I would understand that Mr. Coric would be critical to that investigation. It was important to understand that it was one of his offices at the base of the flats from where these people were taken. Yes, if there had been investigation, yes, there should be some findings even if the findings don't reach conclusions on who was responsible. At that stage I could see no particular evidence for there having been an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any reports connected to that investigation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Could we put on the ELMO document 5D 00523. The heading reads "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council, Defence Department." In the left-hand corner, it says: "Administration of the military police," and there is a number and a date: "Mostar, the 9th of February, 1993." The title is "Special report with respect to the arrest and transport of 13 persons of Serb nationality on the Mostar-Stolac route." And if we could scroll down and look at the signature. It says that the signatory is Chief Dragan Barbaric, and there is the seal of the military police administration. Could you please tell us whether you have ever seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now show in e-court document number 5D 00524 [as interpreted]. We have some technical problems. This is not the document. Could we put it on the ELMO, please. I do apologise. I've been told that it's wrong in the record. I'm going for 5D 00534. This is the document. It's a document which again has the heading "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council." And on the left-hand side it says: "Ministry of Defence, SIS Centre Mostar." And then there is the registration number, and the date is Mostar, 7th of December, 1993. I would like to read to you parts of that document. "Pursuant to Article 151, paragraph 2 of the law on criminal procedure, authorised officers of the Mostar SIS centre in the presence of a recording clerk are composing the following minutes: "About information provided on the 6th of December, 1992, by Vukasin Batinic, son of Djordje and Zora, nee Kostic," and then the details of this person follow, which I will skip over, and he's a resident in Ante Zvanic Street, number 15D. "On 5th of February, 1993, at around 1200 hours, I was sitting with my family in my flat, and our neighbour Ivanka was there as well. Two soldiers came in wearing camouflage uniforms without any visible insignia showing to what unit they belonged." The end of that paragraph reads: "From there they took us on the road towards Rastani. We passed by the hydroelectric power plant in Mostar, and we took the road to Stolac. When we arrived in Stolac, they found a white sheet and a stick and took us to Begovina. This is area between Stolac and Berkovici towards the Serbian lines. "They stopped us, gave us the white flag, and said, 'Go to your people. If they don't kill you, we will.'" Tell me, Mr. Beese, in your statement you said that you questioned witnesses to the events in Stolac. I have abbreviated this because we don't have time for me to read the whole statement to you, but does this part of the statement refer to that incident in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I will now read to you another part of the statement, which reads as follows: "My wife and I have firmly decided to go back. I heard over the radio of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna that we were expelled by an unauthorised group and that we can return without any problems. We contacted UNPROFOR and kept asking about how we could return to Mostar. We succeeded in this on the 3rd of December, 1993, when we returned along the same road over which we were expelled, in an exchange. We cried with joy and on arrival in Mostar in our home we found our daughter Vanja and saw that none of our belongings were missing." And the last passage says: "I don't have any objections to the work of the officers of SIS in Mostar. Everything I have said has been correctly entered into the record, which I confirm with my own signature." And then there follows his signature, Vukasin Batinic, and this is also signed by Zoran Lasic, the head of the SIS office in Mostar, and it has an official seal. In connection with these documents which we've seen, as far as I was able to understand, you discussed this event with Mr. Coric a few weeks or a month after the event occurred. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Subsequently, in the period up to July, 1993, which I understand is the time you spent in Bosnia, did you subsequently again inquire about the investigation in this case with Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you then allow for the possibility that there was an investigation which was completed after you had left Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date of the statement you've shown me is December, which is after I left Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the statement doesn't answer the fundamental questions as to how the event happened in the first place or what efforts had been made to discover how it could have happened. And I'm not talking about the criminal activity that is alleged to have happened in the report but how it was possible for these things to happen without official involvement of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Do you allow for the possibility that an investigation was initiated and continued to be conducted after you left the area? Why, then, would anyone inform you of it after you had left Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move on. In your statement, you mentioned that you spoke to Mr. Coric about a transport of prisoners in an ambulance. Do you remember having mentioned that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see such a transport?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where and when?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the -- outside the office of Mr. Prlic, some hundred metres to the west of his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And where were you at that point in time when you were looking at the vehicle? How far away from it were you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty-five metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether the vehicle was a van or did it have a canvas? What type of vehicle was it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a -- of the size of a van. If I recall correctly, it was green and carried hospital markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you see what the persons inside the van were wearing? And how did you see this? Was the door open? You saw it from a distance of 25 metres. What were the uniforms like?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The uniforms were fairly ragged military camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the insignia on these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't appear to have any insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, then, how you came to conclude that they were prisoners.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The camouflage uniforms used by the different units were not exactly the same. Although these were faded and battered, they looked much more like the uniforms that were in use with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The fact they were getting in and out nowhere near a hospital, the fact that their demeanour showed them to be more captive and they were covered by armed men rather than injured, with bandages or anything else, suggested that they were prisoners and not wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you approach any closer and take a closer look at these people? Did you ask them what was going on?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Could we then say that it was merely your assumption that these were prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions about this. Now, I wish to move on to another topic. Among the other topics you discussed with Mr. Coric, according to your statement, you also discussed Mujahedin. You stated that Valentin Coric complained about extremist Muslim elements, Mujahedin, in Central Bosnia, and that you told him, How could they have arrived in Central Bosnia when passage to Central Bosnia is controlled by the HVO at checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree -- I will not use the word "Mujahedin." I will use the word "volunteers" from Islamic countries, extreme Muslims. Do you know that there were such people fighting in the ranks of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the time period we are now discussing in Central Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you accept that or deny it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation was quite specifically that there were those people in Central Bosnia, that they had, some of them, entered as aid workers, which meant moving through HVO territory. Mr. Coric referred to them as Mujahedin, not me, and I offered the view that if they were coming through HVO territory, the HVO had some control, perhaps, of their flow. I'm sorry if my account didn't come across that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please -- I still don't have an answer to my question. My question was: Do you consider that on the territory of Central Bosnia there were extreme elements who were volunteers from Islamic countries or not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So there were such people there. Thank you. Excuse me. Yes. We have now clarified a situation where you say that in relation to the arrival of these extreme elements into Central Bosnia Mr. Coric complained to you and you said to him that it was the HVO that were supposed to control the roads leading to Central Bosnia and prevent such extreme elements from entering the territory. Is this the conclusion we've reached from all this? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "supposed to" control is not correct. Whether they should or should not, they did control the roads; therefore, they had some means of control.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me what those means of control were and on what roads.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO controlled movement on all roads leading from the coast, where aid entered the country, to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, now, as you have military experience - and in Northern Ireland there were also extreme conditions, I think you will agree with me that the conditions in Bosnia and Herzegovina were no better than those in Northern Ireland - while you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in your statement where you describe your job in Northern Ireland, you say that under those conditions for security you had to control the flow of people and vehicles. When you say "in those conditions," do you mean dangerous conditions similar to wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dangerous conditions, though the conditions in Bosnia were a good deal worse than those in Northern Ireland at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, do you allow for the possibility that under the pretext of humanitarian aid some persons from a criminal milieu in Bosnia and Herzegovina attempted to engage in smuggling, black marketeering, and so on? Do you allow for the possibility of that happening?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Also, in view of your statement about the possibility of preventing the passage of extreme elements, do you agree with me that such passage had to be checked at HVO checkpoints by checking the identity of persons passing through the checkpoints? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know that the HVO military police, together with the International Red Cross Committee, discussed ways for the convoy carrying humanitarian aid to pass through with the aim of preventing the abuse by persons who were not authorised to travel in such convoys and engage in traffickeering and things like that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the following document now, please: 5D 00524. It says as the heading "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council, Defence Department." And on the left-hand side, "Administration office of the military police," the number. And it says "Mostar, the 5th of February, 1993." The signatory of this order -- may we zoom -- or, rather, see the document at the bottom. It says "Valentin Coric," as chief, and on the left-hand side, it was delivered to, under 5, the ICRC Committee. In the document it says the following: "In conformity with the agreement by authorised representatives of the ICRC and the head of the military police department of the 4th of February, 1993, linked to the passage of humanitarian aid convoys organised by the ICRC, I hereby order: That as of the 7th of February, 1993, the following regime be established: The ICRC is duty-bound to give notification of passing convoys on telephone or facsimile at least 24 hours before the passing of the convoy. "2. Notification of the route;" And 3, that a list of names will be handed over, three copies, travel list. So those are the contents of this order as related to the convoy. I'm going to show you a number of documents first and then I'll come to my question. So the next document is 5D 00525. I think we have prepared that document for the ELMO. This is the document. You can see the telefax that arrived from the ICRC chief in Metkovic on the 9th of February, 1993. And it reads as follows: "With this I inform you of the unfortunate incident that occurred this morning around 10.00 hours in Capljina, and what we are prepared to undertake: "Sequel of the event is as follows: "Humanitarian aid sent to Capljina on three trucks in height of about 75 tonnes of food around 10.00 hours this morning on 9 February, 1993, stopped by the military police and taken to the circle of the barracks in Capljina. Drivers were taken and trucks impounded. First information came to me when one of the drivers reached the telephone and informed me about it. After my arrival in the barracks in Capljina, we were left to wait more than half an hour for the commander of the military police, Mr. Kraljevic, who did not show up even after that. In the meantime, the drivers were released from the detention in the circle of the barracks. I left a message to Mr. Kraljevic that we expect his official apology tonight in circle of UNHCR Metkovic, and that if the drivers and the trucks are not released immediately, all the aid to Herceg-Bosna will be suspended until further notice as of tomorrow." And linked to that document I'd like to display one more document to be placed on the ELMO. 5D 00526 is the number. The heading once again, "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council." The letter is addressed to the UNHCR of Metkovic on the 9th of February, 1993. The signatory is Mr. Valentin Coric. "Respected gentlemen, in regards to the above enclosed fax, we inform you that this incident occurred due to misunderstanding for which part of the blame is borne by both sides. The fax we received did not have the exact address of the receiver of the aid but only the city of Capljina. Considering that we had information that a convoy with smuggled goods that supposed to be used for criminal actions ... will come across the Doljani border, which is not intended for the members of the units but criminals using it for plunder of the population of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Kraljevic was on an official trip so that we kept your convoy longer. "We apologise for all the unpleasantness that you have met with and I hope that this incident will not influence the cooperation between the UNHCR and the military police of the HVO for the benefit of the people living in Herceg-Bosna." Now, after you've seen those three documents, would you agree with me when I say that it is possible that the convoy was held back at the checkpoints because the individuals transporting the humanitarian aid did not have the right papers or did not report their arrival beforehand, so that there was misunderstanding and complications with regard to the passage of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have two more documents to show you now. They are 5D 00529. That's the first document. The document is once again the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council, military police, 3rd Battalion of the 3rd Company. We have a number - again I don't want to read it out - and the date is the 9th of February, 1993. And the signatory is Ivan Ancic, who compiled the report, report made by. And the text states as follows, may we zoom up: "During the day a military police patrol from -- took in from Gabela point ten cargo vehicles loaded with boards and wooden material in total amount of 88.316 cubic metres, the leader of the convoy was Eljub Cakovic." The second paragraph, at the end of it, I'd like to read now: "The vehicles were moving from the direction of Olovo towards Metkovic but did not go to the main border with the intent of avoiding customs so they were returned to the barracks and after that sent to the administration office of the military police, where they were released, and last night they were noticed selling material from the trucks on a roundabout in Ljubuski. It was pure smuggling." Having read that, in your opinion could that be the smuggling incident that I asked you about several minutes ago when you said that you agreed with me that it was necessary to control the checkpoints to avoid smuggling, to control the goods at the checkpoint to avoid smuggling? Could that be an attempt of that kind?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to read out paragraph 3 of this document: "A vehicle Mercedes 12/3 was taken in from Doljani, registration place MO 172-813 with a cargo of humanitarian aid for Mostar with the driver Nusret Mustovic with blank confirmation issued by Jadran Topic dated the 21st of December, 1992, without a packing list and without destination as to who is the receiver of the goods." Would you agree with me that this event, the one that I just read out, referred to cargo being transported but without the necessary papers and documents since we said that there was blank confirmation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: May we have document 5D 00528 now, please. The heading is the same as on the previous document, and so is the date, and the report was compiled once again by Ivan Ancic and this is what paragraph 2 says: "During the day a truck of the Mercedes 12-12 type was checked, registration plates MO 172-813, transporting humanitarian aid. A statement was taken, the data checked, and the vehicle was released to continue its journey towards Mostar." I'd just like us to take note of the fact that it was a vehicle which in the previous report which was described - judging from the licence plates we can tell that it's the same vehicle - and that it was stopped to check the data. That concludes my cross-examination. I'd like to thank you, Mr. Beese. I don't know whether Mr. Valentin Coric would like to ask you any questions. He did ask for a few minutes of our time earlier on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric. Go ahead, please. We have 15 minutes left. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Beese, you said that we met four or five times; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: My Defence counsel has more or less recounted the contents of our discussions or talks. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: On a number of occasions you complimented me on my English. Do you happen to remember whether we had an interpreter while we were talking?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that latter occasion I believe we did. Present with us, not necessarily acting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to comment on something that I think needs to be said after the cross-examination by my Defence counsel. You stressed that I spoke about the problem of foreigners, foreign warriors in Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that four escorts of the brigade commander from Zenica, Zivko Totic, were killed at a checkpoint in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you know who killed those men?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were an extreme Muslim group.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: So you remember that the official position of the BH army was that that was perpetrated by the Mujahedin; is that right? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that word was used, but -- but extreme elements, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll use "extreme elements," two words instead of the one. Now, do you know what happened afterwards, after the killing of those four military policemen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Totic was later exchanged. He was handed -- handed back and freed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you know who he was exchanged for?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Who was released and who --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, or I'll try and jog your memory. He was exchanged for six extremist Muslims, and later plus two, which makes eight. Did you write about that in your report? Or perhaps your colleagues did.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present in Zenica on the day that that exchange took place, and the account from which some of the extracts of Defence counsel's questioning today has been taken from is more of an account of my time. It's not meant to be an exclusive -- sorry, inclusive history of all events.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: One of those extreme Muslims. I'd like document 5D 00527 to be placed on the ELMO now, please. Do we have the document? So I shall begin. As you can see, the document is from the administration office of the military police, department for political activity, Ljubuski. The date is the 7th of November, 1993. It says: "Number of persons killed, wounded and missing or arrested members of the military police of the HVO HR HB." This document speaks about the casualties from among the military police for the whole of Herceg-Bosna from the beginning of the war up until roughly the moment that I left the military police. So everything that I am going to read out took place when I was the number one man in the military police. I'm going to read the final figures, not the others. During that period, roughly speaking, the military police numbered between 700 to 2.000-odd members during that period of time. And during that time, 152 members of the military police were killed, 565 persons were wounded, and persons who had disappeared or were arrested, 52. This document was signed by Pavle Loncar, the head of the PD department. And these figures, with photographs, can be found in an official document of this court, which is a military police manual. If we look at a battalion in Central Bosnia, where the concentration of those extremist Muslims and religious fighters was greatest, who had come in as humanitarian workers, you will see that almost 50 per cent of the casualties took place precisely in that area over there. Now, do you think that I had reason enough to caution you and to tell you to take into account that fact already at the beginning of 1993? Do you understand me today if you failed to understand me at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I do see the importance of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Is it clear to you that I wasn't politicising or dramatising the situation without reason, for no reason at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Then I have to ask you another question. In your observations at various places, did you come to proclaim the military police almost as a political organisation? Did -- were those people killed at rostrums, perhaps, while we were speaking? I don't think so, and I'm sure you'll agree with me on that point, won't you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you know that many military policemen lost their lives precisely at checkpoints where they were controlling the passage of people and goods, that they were brutally killed by shelling or whatever, and you were a witness yourself in Bosnia at that junction at Nova Bila. Do you remember that incident at Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I have had very positive experiences from our wartime

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that certain events are seen better close up than from a distance. You would agree, wouldn't you? We worked together a great deal at the time, didn't we? But let's leave that alone for now, although I can't keep silent, and I do understand my Defence counsel when she was very emotional when she referred to the insults you hurled at the Croats in Herzegovina. Why did you choose Siroki Brijeg for living in if it was so bad? Why didn't you go to Jablanica? Was your security and safety good or bad at that time there? Did those people insult you, perhaps? Did they perhaps attack you in any way?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The choice of Siroki Brijeg was made before I arrived. However, it was a convenient position from which to work into Mostar. At the time, it was seen to be more important that we engaged with the senior officials at the HVO and others in Mostar than those in the provincial towns. The people of Siroki Brijeg, some were very hospitable, some were certainly not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to clarify one more point. In -- you say at one point when the people of Siroki Brijeg go to Germany, they go to their patrons. What do you mean by "patrons"? What did you mean when you used that word?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a derogatory word at all. It was simply that there was a sound relationship between the people of that area who worked as guest workers in Germany as opposed to anywhere else. Certainly not a derogatory term.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I don't think you're being honest, sincere. I was very grateful to my own patrons, but it was my impression when I read that that you were alluding to World War II. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A special relationship between Herzegovina, say, for instance, and Germany may endure for many years. I was referring specifically at that time to the relationship between Germany and Herzegovina for guest workers in the years prior to the conflict in Bosnia. That is, the more recent one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- you know that I cannot be satisfied with your answer, and I don't think other people would be satisfied either, but I'd just like to remind you of this, that most of the people of Herzegovina went to Germany and other countries of Western Europe and America - there are more people living over there than there are living in my village - just to survive, to have bread to eat, not for political patronage or any other patronage. And if you didn't know the truth before, I'm telling you now. The people of Herzegovina -- or Herzegovina was not a state. It was an area which suffered greatly and had to go through very harsh times during the times of Yugoslavia, and that's why they had to leave. So I thank you for your cooperation, more your wartime cooperation with me than your cooperation now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 7.00 p.m., which means that we have concluded business for today. We shall reconvene tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.
